newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's Ssangyong may sell headquarters-company.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's Ssangyong may sell headquarters-company.

text.p: In what would be a symbolically devastating move, Ssangyong Motor Co Ltd said on Wednesday it may sell its headquarter building and other assets to pay off heavy debts.
"We need 400 to 500 billion won ($450-$560 million) to meet short-term financial requirements," said Lee Sang-chun, a spokesman for South Korea's fourth-largest carmaker.
Ssangyong's surprise announcement follows a similar asset sale plan unveiled on Tuesday by the troubled Jinro Group, the nation's 19th-largest conglomerate.

There have been fears of a domino-effect of corporate failures since Hanbo Steel Co collapsed in January and Sammi Steel went under in March. Credit tightening by banks in the wake of those failures is forcing business groups to cut debt.
Lee said Ssangyong expected some 400 billion won from the sale of the headquarters in southern Seoul, a wheel disc plant and other real estate.
Analysts said Ssangyong accumulated 3.7 trillion won of debts after investing heavily to develop new vehicles, paying more than 300 billion won in interest annually.
The company has put its debts at 3.2 trillion won.
The troubled automaker posted a net loss of 228.5 billion won in 1996, against a shortfall of 126.2 billion in 1995.
Ssangyong, a specialised maker of four wheel-drive utility vehicles, poured about two trillion won into developing four models in a technical tie-up with Mercedes-Benz, a subsidiary of Daimler-Benz.
The German auto company has a 2.6 percent stake in Ssangyong Motor, a subsidiary of the Ssangyong Group, Korea's sixth largest.
These models include the Musso and New Korando sport utility vehicles, and the Chairman luxury sedan, which will go on sale late this year.
Ssangyong Motor earlier said it was in talks with U.S. giant General Motors Corp over a strategic alliance in which the U.S. firm would inject cash in return for using Ssangyong's sales network.

Nam Seung-soo, an analyst at Daishin Economic Research Institute, said the sale indicated the depth of Ssangyong's woes, but may not solve the cash problem. "Ssangyong must be desperate for cash. Sell-offs of buildings and lands will not be enough to rescue the stricken Ssangyong," he said.
He said all Korean automakers were hurting because of lagging domestic vehicle sales and slowing exports. The weak yen has made Japanese cars more competitive in global markets.
Hyundai Motor Co Ltd, South Korea's largest car maker, said it has cut production due to rising inventories.

"About two-thirds of Ssangyong's debts should be repaid within a year. If the Ssangyong Group really wants to save the auto unit, it may have to sell off some other subsidiaries," said Hur Kang, an analyst at Hyundai Securities.
The group has 25 subsidiaries.
On Tuesday, the Jinro Group, also announced it would sell off businesses, including its canned food and soft drink lines, and other assets because of financial pressures.

Jinro, Korea's largest producer of distilled spirits, said in a statement it would raise a total of 1.2 trillion won by the end of 1998 to bring its equity-to-asset ratio to 24.7 percent from the current 4.43 percent.
Analysts said Jinro's debts exceeded three trillion won.
Corporate failures, which flared with the collapse of the Hanbo Group's Hanbo Steel Co in January under $5.8 billion in debts, have revealed fundamental weaknesses in South Korea's economy.
Sammi Steel, flagship of the Sammi Group, failed in March because of heavy debt.
